content: The recommendations are intended to guide healthcare professionals in the management of childbirth, labor, and the postpartum period across all healthcare settings. These recommendations are specifically targeted at healthcare providers involved in developing national and local health policies related to childbirth and postpartum care, as well as those directly providing care to women during and after childbirth. This includes midwives, nurses, general practitioners, obstetricians, and managers of maternal and child health programs. Additionally, professional societies, non-governmental organizations promoting woman-centered maternity care, and implementers of maternal and child health programs may also find these recommendations relevant. The primary focus of the recommendations is the detection and treatment of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH). Key questions guiding the evidence synthesis and decision-making process are structured using the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) format. For example, one question examines whether specific methods for assessing postpartum blood loss improve the detection of PPH and maternal and perinatal outcomes compared to other methods. Another question evaluates whether the use of care bundles for women experiencing PPH improves outcomes compared to usual care or care bundles with different components. The population affected by these recommendations includes women giving birth and those experiencing PPH in low-, middle-, and high-resource settings. The recommendations were developed following standardized procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. This process involved identifying priority questions, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination, implementation, and evaluation. In 2023, the development of WHO recommendations on PPH detection and treatment using care bundles was identified as a high priority. Six main groups participated in this process, each with specific roles. The WHO Steering Group, composed of WHO staff from relevant departments, managed the updating process, drafted key questions, identified systematic review teams and guideline methodologists, and supervised evidence synthesis. They also organized meetings, finalized the recommendation document, and managed its dissemination and implementation. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) included experts in research, clinical practice, policy, and program development, as well as patient and consumer representatives. This group appraised and interpreted evidence, formulated final recommendations, and reviewed the final document. The Evidence Synthesis Group (ESG) conducted or updated systematic reviews, appraised evidence, and developed Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) frameworks. They also provided technical expertise during GDG meetings. External partners and observers, including representatives from international organizations such as USAID, ICM, FIGO, and Unitaid, participated in the GDG meeting as observers. These organizations collaborate with WHO in guideline dissemination and implementation. The External Review Group (ERG), composed of technical experts, reviewed the final document for factual accuracy, clarity, and contextual relevance. They ensured that decision-making processes incorporated the values and preferences of affected populations, healthcare professionals, and policymakers. Evidence to support the recommendations was derived from systematic reviews conducted by review teams in collaboration with the WHO Steering Group. For effectiveness, WHO commissioned an update of a systematic review on postpartum blood loss assessment and a new review on the effectiveness of care bundles for PPH treatment. Evidence on the diagnostic accuracy of different methods for assessing postpartum blood loss was also synthesized. The systematic review on care bundles included studies evaluating interventions combining three or more components used concurrently or collectively. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-RCTs, interrupted time series studies, and before-after studies. The review considered studies from all income settings without language restrictions. The quality of included studies was assessed using tools such as the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for RCTs and the ROBINS-I tool for non-RCTs. A 2023 qualitative evidence synthesis (QES) explored the perceptions and experiences of women, community members, and healthcare workers regarding PPH prevention, detection, and management. This review provided evidence on acceptability, feasibility, and equity. Additionally, a systematic review of economic evaluations synthesized evidence on the cost-effectiveness of interventions for PPH prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. The certainty of evidence for effectiveness was assessed using the GRADE approach, considering factors such as study design limitations, inconsistency, indirectness, and imprecision. The quality of studies included in the QES was assessed using an adapted version of the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) tool. The cost-effectiveness review used the extended Consensus on Health Economic Criteria list to assess the quality of economic evaluations.
